chunks: What is a GPU. The question: What is a GPU?
A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a processor built to do a huge number of simple, similar calculations at the same time.
A CPU has a few powerful cores that each run one task fast. A GPU has thousands of small, simple arithmetic units, called lanes.
It was made to color the millions of pixels on a screen, and the same design now also speeds up science and AI.
Imagine painting a giant mural made of 8 million tiny squares. One master painter works fast but still does one square at a time.
A crowd of 10,000 helpers, each painting one square at a time from the same simple instructions, finishes far sooner, even though each helper is slower. A GPU is that crowd.
Not to scale and schematic. The CPU spends most of its area on cache and control logic to make one thread fast.
The GPU spends area on arithmetic lanes and register files and on a wide memory interface, accepting that each thread is slower.
Throughput: total work finished per second, as opposed to how fast one task finishes. Thread: one independent stream of work, such as the program for one pixel.
Shader: the small program run for each pixel, each triangle corner (vertex) or each compute thread. SIMT: single instruction, multiple threads.
Groups of threads run the same instruction together. Memory bandwidth: how many bytes per second can move between memory and the chip.
A 4K frame is 3840 times 2160 equals 8 294 400 pixels, about 8. 3 million. At 60 frames per second that is about 498 million pixels per second.
Assume 300 arithmetic operations per pixel, counting extra drawing and effects. That is roughly 150 billion operations per second.
Each pixel can be shaded without waiting for its neighbors. A modern GPU delivers tens of trillions of operations per second, so this is a modest share.
That is the whole idea: independent work spread across many lanes.

"A GPU is a throughput-oriented parallel processor with thousands of small lanes that run the same program on many threads at once, backed by very high memory bandwidth and fixed-function graphics units.
Graphics is perfect for it because millions of pixels are independent. It hides memory latency with massive multithreading instead of big caches.
Today the same hardware also runs compute and machine learning."
